titleStmt.title: Global EDF schedulability analysis of arbitrary sporadic task systems

analytic.title: Global EDF schedulability analysis of arbitrary sporadic task systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Recent results on the global multiprocessor EDF scheduling of sporadic task systems are, for the most part, applicable only to task systems in which each task's relative deadline parameter is constrained to be no larger than its period. This paper introduces new analysis techniques that allow for similar results to be derived for task systems in which individual tasks are not constrained in this manner.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The sporadic task model [16,9] is one of the more commonly used formal models for representing recurring real-time task systems. In this paper, we consider real-time systems that are modeled by the sporadic task model and implemented upon a platform comprised of several identical fully preemptive processors. We assume that the platform allows for global interprocessor migration -a job may begin execution on any processor and a preempted job may resume execution on any processor. (However, each job may execute on at most one processor at each instant in time.)

This paper considers the behavior of the wellknown Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling algorithm [15,12] when scheduling systems of sporadic tasks upon such platforms. A large number of interesting and important results have recently been obtained concerning the multiprocessor EDF scheduling of sporadic task systems under the global paradigm of interprocessor migration (see, e.g., [1,2,11,10,4,5]). However, these results are for the most part applicable only to constrained-deadline sporadic task systemstask systems in which each task's relative deadline parameter is guaranteed to be no larger than its minimum inter-arrival separation ("period") parameter. This is because while at most one job of each task may be pending at each time-instant in constrained deadline systems, multiple jobs of the same task may be simultaneously pending if individual jobs' deadlines exceed the minimum inter-arrival time of successive jobs, and previous analysis techniques have not been able to deal with multiple simultaneously pending jobs from a single task. (While some prior techniques have indeed been extended to handle non constrained-deadline systems, they typically employ the artifact of replacing each task's relative deadline parameter by the smaller of its relative deadline and its period; this artifact introduces significant pessimism and the resulting schedulability conditions are not conducive to the kinds of quantitative analysis we conduct in this paper.) tems continue to hold for arbitrary task systems; i.e., there appears to be no loss in schedulability in moving from the constrained-deadline model to the more general arbitrary model.

Organization. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we formally define the sporadic task model and provide some additional useful definitions. In Section 3, we briefly describe some related research. In Section 4 we derive, and prove the correctness of, a global-EDF schedulability test for arbitrary sporadic task systems. In Section 5 we provide a quantitative characterization of the efficacy of this new schedulability test in terms of the processor speedup metric.

div.head: Model
div.p: A sporadic task τ i = (C i , D i , T i ) is characterized by a worst-case execution requirement C i , a (relative) deadline D i , and a minimum inter-arrival separation parameter T i , also referred to as the period of the task. Such a sporadic task generates a potentially infinite sequence of jobs, with successive job-arrivals separated by at least T i time units. Each job has a worst-case execution requirement equal to C i and a deadline that occurs D i time units after its arrival time. We refer to the interval, of size D i , between such a job's arrival instant and deadline as its scheduling window. We assume a fully preemptive execution model: any executing job may be interrupted at any instant in time, and its execution resumed later with no cost or penalty. A sporadic task system is comprised of several such sporadic tasks. Let τ denote a system of such sporadic tasks:
div.formula: τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . τ n }, with τ i = (C i , D i , T i ) for all i, 1 ≤ i ≤ n.
div.p: Task system τ is said to be a constraineddeadline sporadic task system if it is guaranteed that each task τ i ∈ τ has its relative deadline parameter no larger than its period:
div.formula: D i ≤ T i for all τ i ∈ τ .
div.p: Priority-driven scheduling algorithms operate as follows: at each instant in time they assign a priority to each job that is awaiting execution, and choose for execution the jobs with the greatest priority. The Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling algorithm [15,12] is a priority-driven scheduling algorithm that assigns priority to jobs according to their absolute deadlines: the earlier the deadline, the greater the priority.

With respect to a given platform, a given sporadic task system is said to be feasible if there exists a schedule meeting all deadlines for every collection of jobs that may be generated by the task system. A given sporadic task system is said to be (global) EDF schedulable if EDF meets all deadlines for every collection of jobs that may be generated by the task system. While every EDF-schedulable task system is trivially feasible, it is known that not all feasible task systems are EDF-schedulable.
We find it convenient to define some properties and parameters for individual sporadic tasks, and for sporadic task systems.

Processor speedup factors. Upon preemptive uniprocessors, EDF is known to be an optimal scheduling algorithm in the sense that it can meet all deadlines for any feasible task system. Upon multiprocessors, it has been shown [13] that no on-line algorithm for scheduling sporadic task systems can be optimal in this sense. Since optimality is unachievable, processor speedup factor is a widely-used metric for evaluating the goodness of on-line algorithms for scheduling sporadic task systems.

Definition 1 (Processor speedup factor) A scheduling algorithm is defined to have a processor speedup factor f , f ≥ 1, if, for any task system that is feasible upon a specific multiprocessor platform, the algorithm schedules the task system to meet all deadlines upon a platform comprised of the same number of processors in which each processor is faster by a factor f .

The smaller the processor speedup factor associated with an algorithm, the better it is; in the terminology of processor speedup factor, an optimal algorithm has a processor speedup factor equal to one.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Baker [1,2,11] designed a test from first principles for global-EDF schedulability analysis of sporadic task systems. In essence, Baker's test -henceforth referred to here as the [BAK] test -is obtained by assuming that a task τ k 's job misses its deadline, and then determining necessary conditions on the parameters of all the tasks that must be satisfied in order for such a deadline miss to occur. Then negating these conditions for each τ k yields a sufficient test for global-EDF schedulability.

In 2005, Bertogna et al. [11] used ideas very similar to Baker's to come up with a simpler test that occasionally outperforms the [BAK] tests. The test from [11] will be referred to here as the [BCL] test.

div.head: Overview of the [BAK] and [BCL] tests.
div.p: Both tests are built around the following general strategy, first introduced by Baker [1]. Suppose that τ is not global EDF-schedulable, and consider a sequence of job requests of τ on which global EDF misses one or more deadlines. Suppose that a job of τ k is the first job that misses its deadline, at some time-instant t d . Both tests analyze the situation over some time interval [t o , t d ), where t o is different in the [BAK] and [BCL] tests (and is precisely defined for each test). Both tests compute upper bounds on the amount of work that EDF is required to execute over the interval [t o , t d ), and obtain an unschedulability condition by setting this bound to be large enough to deny τ k 's job C k units of execution over its scheduling window.

In 2007, Bertona and Cirinei [10] extended the response-time analysis technique from uniprocessor scheduling theory to multiprocessors. In essence, the technique in [10] iteratively computes improved bounds on the worst-case response times of jobs, using any of previously known techniques (such as the ones in the [BCL] and [BAK] tests) to determine response times at each iteration.

Quantitative performance bounds. One of the drawbacks of all the above sufficient schedulability tests is that they do not come with quantitative metrics -it is not possible to compare the different tests other than via extensive simulations on artificially-generated test data.
Phillips et al. [17] studied the global EDF scheduling of specified collections of independent jobs. They obtained the following quantitative result for global EDF:

div.p: Theorem 1 (from [17]) Global EDF is optimal to within a processor speedup factor of (2 -1 m ) in the scheduling of collections of independent jobs. That is, any collection of independent jobs that can be scheduled to meet all deadlines upon m processors of a given speed will meet all deadlines if scheduled using global EDF upon m processors each of which is at least (2 -1 m ) times as fast.

This is an interesting and important result, but in order to apply it to sporadic task systems we would first need to determine whether a given sporadic task system is feasible. Unfortunately, no exact feasibility tests are currently known for arbitrary (or even constraineddeadline) sporadic task systems, while the only known non-trivial sufficient tests have all essentially been derived as sufficient schedulability conditions for different scheduling algorithms (such as, for example, the sufficient schedulability conditions for global EDF that we derive in this paper). Implicit-deadline or Liu and Layland task systems are sporadic task systems in which all tasks' relative deadline parameters are equal to their inter-arrival separation parameters (i.e., D i = T i (∀i)). Feasibilityanalysis for such systems is trivial: implicit-deadline sporadic task system τ is feasible upon m unitcapacity processors if and only if u max (τ ) ≤ 1 and u sum (τ ) ≤ m. Since feasibility-analysis can thus be done on implicit-deadline task systems, Theorem 1 may be applied; this was done in [18,14,3]

(This condition was also shown to be tight in the sense that there are implicitdeadline task systems τ with u sum (τ ) exceeding the right-hand side (RHS) of the above condition by an arbitrarily small amount, upon which global EDF misses deadlines.) A characterization of global EDF in terms of processor speedup factor was recently [5] obtained for constrained-deadline sporadic task systems: Theorem 2 (from [5]) Global EDF is optimal to within a processor speedup factor of (3 + √ 5)/2 ≈ 2.62 in the scheduling of constrained-deadline sporadic task systems.

Partitioned EDF scheduling. In contrast to global scheduling, partitioned scheduling assigns each task to a specific processor, and requires that each job execute only upon the processor to which the task generating it has been assigned. Partitioned EDF scheduling algorithms for sporadic task systems are derived in [7]; it is shown that the algorithm for scheduling constrained-deadline sporadic task systems has a processor speedup factor of (3 -1 m ), whereas the one for scheduling arbitrary sporadic task systems has the poorer processor speedup factor of (4 -2 m ). Thus in the partitioned-scheduling case, it appears that one pays a penalty, in the form of an increased processor speedup factor, for the added expressiveness of the arbitrary (non constrained-deadline) model.

div.head: A global-EDF schedulability test
div.p: We now derive (Theorem 3 below) a new schedulability test for arbitrary-deadline sporadic task systems. Our approach towards developing this test is very similar to the approach adopted in [5] for constraineddeadline sporadic task systems, and follows the same general framework as the derivations of the [BAK] and [BCL] tests: we obtain necessary conditions for global EDF to miss a deadline when scheduling sporadic task system τ upon m unit-capacity processors. By taking the contrapositive of these conditions, we obtain a sufficient schedulability condition. The added complication over the derivation in [5] is that multiple jobs of each task may be pending at any given instant in time; hence the techniques used in [5] must be extended (and modified when necessary) in order to apply them to this more general case.

div.head: A processor speedup factor for global EDF
div.p: In [5], the following necessary conditions for any constrained-deadline sporadic task system to be feasible upon a multiprocessor platform were obtained; as we show below, these same necessary feasibility conditions hold for arbitrary sporadic task systems as well: Lemma 4 Any sporadic task system τ that is feasible upon a multiprocessor platform comprised of m speed-x processors must satisfy δ max (τ ) ≤ x and LOAD(τ ) ≤ mx .
Proof Sketch: Suppose that task system τ is feasible upon m speed-x processors. To prove the first condition above, consider each task τ i separately:
• In order to be able to meet all deadlines of τ i if τ i generates jobs exactly T i time units apart, it is necessary that C i /T i ≤ x.
• Since any individual job of τ i can receive at most D i ×x units of execution by its deadline, we must have
div.formula: C i ≤ D i × x; i.e., C i /D i ≤ x.
div.p: Putting both conditions together, we get (C i / min(T i , D i )) ≤ x. Taken over all tasks in τ , this observation yields the first condition.

What is the significance of this speedup result? We already know that global EDF is not an optimal scheduling algorithm. We have also seen that the schedulability test of Theorem 3 is not optimal (except for the special case m = 1). This speedup result tells us that a processor speedup of (3 + √ 5)/2 ≈ 2.618 compensates for both the non-optimality of global EDF and the inexactness of our schedulability test.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Previous sufficient schedulability conditions for global-EDF scheduling of sporadic task systems have primarily focused upon constrained-deadline task systems. This is because task systems that are not constrained-deadline may have multiple jobs of a single task simultaneously pending execution, and techniques were not previously known for dealing with such a multiplicity of jobs from the same task. (Prior techniques that did claim to handle non constraineddeadline task systems generally did so by the artifact of "replacing" each task (C i , D i , T i ) by a constraineddeadline one with parameters (C i , min(D i , T i ), T i ); however, this artifact introduces significant pessimism and the resulting schedulability conditions do not possess non-trivial processor speedup factors.)

In this paper, we have introduced analysis techniques that allow for consideration of multiple jobs of the same task. Using these techniques, we derived a schedulability test for the global EDF scheduling of arbitrary sporadic task systems upon preemptive multiprocessor platforms, that turns out to essentially be identical to the one previously obtained for constrained-deadline task systems. This yields the somewhat surprising conclusion that, in contrast to the situation with respect to partitioned EDF scheduling, there is no performance penalty in doing away with the restriction that all tasks be constrained-deadline.

We believe that the analysis techniques introduced here are novel and important, and that they will prove useful in studying multiprocessor global schedulability for many more general task and machine models, and for different scheduling algorithms. We have recently [6,8] been successful in extending them to fixed-priority scheduling of sporadic task systems, and are working on applying these principles to even more general task models than the sporadic task model.

DBF(τ i , t) is a step function comprised of steps of height C i , with the first step at t = D i and successive steps exactly T i time units apart. It is seen that the graph of δ i lies above the plot for DBF(τ i , t), for all t. (For D i < T i , the graph for δ i touches the plot for DBF(τ i , t) at t = D i ; for D i = T i , the two touch at all integer multiples of T i ; and for D i > T i the two plots never touch.)

By definition, W (t o ) denotes the amount of work that the EDF schedule needs (but fails) to execute over [t o , t d ). This work in W (t o ) arises from two sources: those jobs that arrived at or after t o , and those that arrived prior to t o but have not completed execution in the EDF schedule by time-instant t o .
